content.p: Between mid-August and mid-October 1928, a police constable and a changing group of pastoralists and helpers rode through the desert country north-west of Alice Springs and shot dead an unknown number of Aboriginal people. The reprisals followed the death of a white dingo trapper, Frederick Brooks, at a waterhole called Yurrkuru. The dead were Warlpiri, Anmatyerre and Kaytetye people. The official tally, set by a federal Board of Enquiry, was 31. Aboriginal families, several historians and the pastoralist Randall Stafford, who rode with the party at first, put the real figure far higher.

The only people brought to trial were two Warlpiri men accused of killing Brooks, and they were acquitted. The man who led the patrols, Mounted Constable William George Murray, was never charged. The Board of Enquiry accepted that his party had acted in self-defence. The killings are often described as the last large-scale massacre of Aboriginal people in Australia, and the period is locally referred to as the "killing times".

In 1928 Central Australia was still a frontier. The Coniston lease, on the Warburton River about 250 km north-west of Alice Springs, had been granted to Randall Stafford in 1917 and was stocked four years later. To the west lay the Tanami desert and, to the north, the Lander River country. Wilson and O'Brien, writing in the journal Aboriginal History, say European contact with the region's Warlpiri owners had been slight, with pastoral stations and the Tanami goldfield the only permanent white presence.

From 1924 the region suffered a four-year drought, the worst on record. Barrow Creek received just 3.29 inches of rain in 1928, the lowest reading since records began in 1899. The permanent soaks along the river systems, on which Aboriginal people depended, drew them closer to the settled districts, where cattle fouled the water and settlers complained of spearing and theft. Starvation among Aboriginal people was noted in reports by the Central Australian Government Resident and Police Commissioner, J. C. Cawood, and by two pastoralists. After the killings became public, the Commonwealth sought to establish that the drought was non-existent or negligible, and the Board of Enquiry later found no evidence of starvation.

The settler view of the contest was blunt. The South Australian Register wrote in September 1928 that it would be impossible to develop the country until there was more police protection. Weeks before the killings, according to the missionary F. W. Albrecht, Cawood remarked at Hermannsburg that it was time the Aboriginal people were taught a lesson.

Brooks, aged 61, was an old friend of Stafford. In July 1928 he asked to try dingo scalping on Coniston land. Stafford warned him that he and the Aboriginal woman he lived with had received threats and that it would be unsafe to go beyond a soak about 22 km west of the station. On 2 August Brooks set out with rations, two camels and two Aboriginal assistants, Skipper and Dodger. On the morning of 7 August the two assistants found him dead, half buried in a rabbit burrow, his camp ransacked.

That Aboriginal people killed him is generally accepted; why is not. Most Aboriginal accounts, as summarised by Wilson and O'Brien, say Brooks was in a sexual relationship with one or two Warlpiri women, either improperly or under an arrangement he failed to honour. Warlpiri men told the researchers Peter and Jay Read that Brooks had asked a man called Japanangka, also known as Bullfrog, to let his wife Marungarli wash clothes for him in exchange for food and tobacco. She did not come back and no food arrived, and Japanangka attacked Brooks at dawn. Japanangka's granddaughter said in 1975 that he killed the white man because the white man had stolen his wife. White accounts of the time said Brooks was killed for his flour and tobacco, and Stafford believed a party that had come to kill him and Alice had killed Brooks instead because he crossed their tracks.

Even how the news travelled is unclear. One account says the prospector Bruce Chapman found and reburied the body; another credits Alex Wilson; a third, from the historian Dick Kimber, says an Aboriginal stockman found it a day earlier and warned people to leave the area. Chapman died of meningitis within days of reaching Alice Springs, and Wilson and O'Brien conclude that the answers died with him. By 13 August the story was in the Adelaide newspapers.

Murray was a veteran of the 4th Light Horse who had landed at Gallipoli in May 1915, fought on the Western Front and returned to Australia in 1918. He joined the Northern Territory police in 1919 and took charge at Barrow Creek in 1926. Wilson and O'Brien describe him as having a reputation as a tough and effective constable, and suggest that, with no formal police training, he fell back on military habits when confronted in Warlpiri country.

Not everyone thought well of him. Stafford, speaking to the anthropologist T. G. H. Strehlow in 1932, dismissed Murray's tales of lone heroics before the Board and called him a killer who would never rush into danger by himself. Strehlow's own impression was of a placid, kindly man.

When Alice Springs police heard of the murder on 11 August, Cawood had that morning sent Murray out from Alice Springs to look into cattle-killing complaints. Murray was met on the road, told of Brooks's death and ordered by telephone to go to the scene and arrest those responsible. He reached Coniston on 12 August and had Aboriginal people who came to the station detained and questioned. On 15 August two men, Padygar and Woolingar, arrived at the camp near the homestead. Murray told the Board that the two tried to escape as his trackers, Paddy and Major, arrested them, and that when he ran to the scene Woolingar attacked him and he shot Woolingar above the eye.

Murray's report said he had learned the names of 20 Aboriginal men implicated in the murder. He did not record the names or explain how he got them. On 16 August he left with Stafford, the prospector John Saxby, the labourer Billy Briscoe, Alex Wilson, the men Paddy and Major, and Dodger. Wilson and O'Brien stress that none of the non-police members were sworn in as special constables, which in their words left them as vigilantes.

By Murray's account, the party met about 23 Aboriginal people that day. He ordered them to disarm, they refused, and a fight followed in which four Warlpiri, including one woman, were killed outright and a second woman died within the hour. An Aboriginal account quoted by Wilson and O'Brien gives a different picture of the same encounter: it says Stafford shot a fleeing young woman, was appalled, and withdrew from the party. Stafford told the Board he had left after the first encounter.

On 19 August, on the Lander north of Coniston, Murray reported meeting six people who ignored warnings and threw boomerangs. Three were killed and three wounded who later died. On 22 August two more Warlpiri were killed attempting to escape. That killing was plainly not self-defence, say Wilson and O'Brien, because the tracker Paddy told the Board he had shot a running boy after chasing him over two hills. Three more were killed about 60 km further west. Murray arrested Akirkra on 22 August. On 31 August Woolingar died of his head wound. The official count for this first patrol was 17, and Murray reported on 2 September that this many had been killed. The ABC records that Murray personally admitted to killing at least 17 people.

On 28 August the Broadmeadows station co-owner William "Nugget" Morton was attacked by a group of Warlpiri. Morton said about 15 men set on him and that he fought his way to his revolver. He did not mention in his first statement that he had killed any attackers. Warlpiri oral history, as recorded by Peter and Jay Read, links the attack to Morton's treatment of Aboriginal women, and Strehlow's diaries record allegations of cruelty by Morton towards Aboriginal women and girls.

Murray reached Broadmeadows on 24 September and set out with Morton, Alex Wilson and a small Aboriginal boy. Wilson and O'Brien give the official sequence. Four people were killed at Tomahawk Waterhole on the Lander, two the next day at Circle Well, and eight more several days later on the lower Hanson River, 14 in all. On the evidence of Murray and Morton, 14 of the 15 alleged attackers were found and killed, and Wilson and O'Brien call it an absurd coincidence that only the guilty died in every encounter.

Aboriginal accounts, gathered from survivors decades later, describe camps attacked while people slept and whole camps rounded up. Wilson and O'Brien say that towards the end many of those killed had not heard of the troubles at Coniston and Broadmeadows and were going about their daily business, in one case taking part in a ceremony. The Kaytetye elder Tommy Thompson Kngwarraye recalled that police on horseback followed people's tracks along a creek, shooting as they went, with two Aboriginal trackers showing them where people were. Murray returned to Alice Springs on 18 October and next day wrote a one-page report that gave no number of Warlpiri killed. He later told the Board he wrote it in a great hurry.

Padygar and Akirkra, the two men Murray took into custody, were charged with Brooks's murder. Both were said to have made confessions. According to Wilson and O'Brien they were acquitted after two trials, the first aborted when its jury was discharged, because the evidence of the sole witness, the boy Lala, was inconsistent and their earlier confessions were ruled inadmissible. Murray travelled to Darwin with the prisoners and Lala. The ABC describes the two men as the only people ever to stand trial over Coniston and says they were wrongly accused. The trial drew missionaries' attention to the killing of at least 17 Warlpiri.

Missionary and humanitarian societies lobbied for an inquiry, and the press coverage was hostile. On 27 November the federal government decided to appoint a Board of Enquiry, and it was formally appointed on 13 December. Wilson and O'Brien say its independence was compromised from the outset. Its members were a Queensland police magistrate, A. H. O'Kelly, as chairman; a South Australian police inspector, P. A. Giles; and Cawood, Murray's own superior, who in the authors' view should have been a witness. Missionary representation was refused, though the lay missionary Ernest Kramer was allowed to attend and cross-examine, and Murray was given the same right.

The Board heard 30 witnesses over 18 days. Neither Major nor Alex Wilson was called. The National Film and Sound Archive notes that only one Aboriginal person gave evidence and that no legal counsel was provided for Aboriginal people. The authors also cite an oral history by Gordon Birt, in which Murray is said to have told a fellow officer that he arranged to reach Stafford before the magistrate's party did, so as to tell him what to say. That is a later recollection, not a finding of the Board.

The findings, made public on 30 January 1929, held that in all the cases the shootings were justified as self-defence and that settlers and police had given no provocation. The Board blamed the "Walmulla" people, a western Warlpiri group, who it said were advancing on Coniston to wipe out the settlers, and said there was not a "scintilla of evidence" that the police party was a punitive expedition. It also blamed "unattached Missionaries wandering from place to place" for preaching the equality of man. It found no evidence of starvation. No charges followed.

The authors list what the Board did not test: other killings reported by Warlpiri people, Alex Wilson and Saxby, including at least six more dead at Tippinba; the missing names of the 20 men; the unsworn status of Murray's party; and how those killed on the first patrol were known to be guilty. The chairman's own confidential report, quoted in a departmental memo, said that had regular police rather than settlers made the patrols, the killing would probably not have been on the same scale.

The official figure of 31 is the sum of the two patrols' reports. Beyond it, the estimates differ. The lay missionary Annie Lock wrote a year later that she believed over 70 had been killed, though she did not name her informants. The Aboriginal bushman Walter Smith told Kimber over 200 had died. Stafford told Strehlow in 1932 that the Board was told of 31 killed and that men who rode with Murray said the true figure was at least twice as high. Wilson and O'Brien say they have new information from perpetrators that the total was at least twice the official number. The Australian War Memorial says more than 60. Aboriginal people speaking to the ABC in 2018 put it nearer 100, and survivors' oral histories, as the ABC summarises them, say as many as 170. The National Film and Sound Archive gives a range of 31 to 100.

For the Warlpiri, Anmatyerre and Kaytetye the killings meant grief and cultural dislocation. Many people fled their country and were taken in by other groups, and some have never returned. The Film and Sound Archive notes that this made it easier for pastoralists to extend their holdings. Wilson and O'Brien argue that Coniston emptied the Warlpiri homeland and made the official punitive expedition unacceptable in the Northern Territory. Murray, who lived until 1975, was never punished.

No photographs or film of the killings exist, and the story has been kept alive in oral history, which the Film and Sound Archive says is well known among Aboriginal people in Central Australia and little known among other Australians.

A memorial was unveiled at Yurrkuru, near where Brooks was killed, in September 2003, on the 75th anniversary. With the Central Land Council's support, large numbers gathered, women danced, and descendants of victims and of perpetrators met for the first time. Murray's great-niece, Liza Dale-Hallett, read a statement of sorrow and reconciliation. A second memorial, built in 2008 at Athimpelengkwe (Baxters Well), stands at a spot on the Hanson River, one of the many places where killings took place as the reprisal party travelled north.

In August 2018, on the eve of the 90th anniversary, the Central Land Council's chairman Francis Kelly called for a national day of remembrance for massacres of Indigenous people, comparable to Anzac Day. Some descendants hoped Northern Territory Police Commissioner Reece Kershaw, who was to attend the ceremony at Yurrkuru, would apologise formally. Grunge, writing in 2022, says the commissioner did issue an apology in 2018 on behalf of the officers who took part; the ABC report from before the ceremony says only that some descendants hoped for one.
